Describe the structure, vision, mission, and regulatory mandate of NAICOM.
Identify and explain the key innovations of NIIRA 2025, the legislation it repeals, the new licensing categories it introduces, and its consumer protection architecture.
Describe the licensing requirements for insurers, reinsurers, brokers, agents, Insurtechs, and loss adjusters under NIIRA 2025.
State the minimum capital requirements introduced by NIIRA 2025 for each class of licensed operator and explain the Risk-Based Capital framework.
Explain the recapitalisation programme: its timeline, compliance process, and consequences of non-compliance.
List and describe the compulsory classes of insurance under Nigerian law and explain the available enforcement mechanisms.
Describe the role and governance of the CIIN and explain the professional requirements under NIIRA 2025.
Identify and describe the roles of the principal industry associations: NIA, NCRIB, ILAN, and ARIAN.

blocks.h: Insurance is, at its core, a promise. An insurer collects premium today and undertakes to pay a claim in the future, possibly years or decades hence. The insured cannot verify in advance whether that promise will be kept; she cannot inspect the insurer's balance sheet with the fluency of a financial analyst, she cannot negotiate the policy terms as an equal, and she may not fully understand the product she has purchased. This information asymmetry, combined with the long time horizons of life insurance and the critical importance of the promise being kept in moments of personal vulnerability, creates a compelling case for regulatory oversight.

Insurance regulation in Nigeria exists to correct these market failures. It ensures that insurers are financially capable of honouring their promises (prudential regulation), that they deal with policyholders honestly and fairly (market conduct regulation), that new entrants meet minimum standards of competence and capitalisation (licensing), and that the system as a whole contributes to rather than undermines economic stability (systemic regulation). These objectives are pursued by the National Insurance Commission (NAICOM) under the legal framework established by NIIRA 2025, the most comprehensive insurance legislation in Nigeria's history.

This chapter traces the regulatory framework from its colonial origins to its current form, examines the structure and mandate of NAICOM, dissects the key provisions of NIIRA 2025, explains the capital requirements and recapitalisation programme, and surveys the ecosystem of industry associations and professional bodies that operate alongside the statutory regulator.

blocks.text: 4.2  Historical Development of Insurance Regulation in Nigeria

blocks.h: Insurance in colonial Nigeria was an unregulated activity conducted principally by agents of British insurance companies, with no dedicated Nigerian legislation, no licensing requirement, and no capital adequacy framework. Premiums flowed to London; so, frequently, did claims disputes. The absence of regulatory infrastructure reflected the limited scope and purpose of insurance in the colonial economy, it existed primarily to serve the commercial interests of British trading companies and the larger Nigerian commercial enterprises that emerged in the 1940s and 1950s. Individual Nigerians had virtually no access to insurance products.

blocks.text: 4.2.2  Post-Independence: The JC Obande Commission and the Insurance Act 1961

blocks.h: Following Nigeria's independence on 1 October 1960, the Federal Government constituted the J.C. Obande Commission of Enquiry into the Insurance Industry in 1961, the first systematic review of insurance in independent Nigeria. Its report documented the dominance of foreign insurers, the near-total absence of indigenous capacity, the lack of regulatory oversight, and the exposure of Nigerian policyholders to insurers of uncertain financial strength.<sup>[1]</sup>

The Commission's recommendations led directly to the Insurance Act 1961, the first comprehensive insurance legislation in independent Nigeria. The Act established the legal framework for licensing companies, brokers, and agents; required foreign insurers to incorporate locally; and vested regulatory oversight in the Ministry of Trade. It was foundational but limited: enforcement was weak, capitalisation requirements were nominal, and actuarial oversight was minimal.

blocks.title: Timeline: Chronology of Nigerian Insurance Regulation

blocks.h: 1961 Insurance Act 1961. First comprehensive legislation post-independence. Licensing framework; local incorporation of foreign insurers.
1969 Insurance (Miscellaneous Provisions) Decree 1969. Extended provisions; addressed premium remittance and local content.
1976 Insurance Decree 1976. Strengthened local content; increased penalties for unregistered operations.
1988 Insurance Decree 40 of 1988. Consolidated decrees; introduced provisions specific to life assurance.
1991 NCRIB Act No. 21 of 1991. Mandated NCRIB membership for all brokers; gave NCRIB self-regulatory powers.
1993 CIIN Act No. 22 of 1993. Chartered the Insurance Institute of Nigeria; established professional qualification and registration framework.
1997 National Insurance Commission Act (Decree No. 1 of 1997). Established NAICOM as apex regulator, replacing NISB. Inaugurated 22 January 1997.
2003 Insurance Act 2003 (Cap. I17, LFN 2004). Comprehensive consolidation; 'no premium, no cover'; capital adequacy; corporate governance. Primary legislation for over two decades.
2022 National Health Insurance Authority Act 2022. Established mandatory health insurance for all Nigerians; replaced NHIS with NHIA.

2025 NIIRA 2025 (Act No. 2, 2025). Presidential assent 31 July 2025. Most comprehensive insurance legislation in Nigeria's history. Consolidates and repeals five prior statutes. Introduces RBC, Insurtech licensing, IPPF, and enhanced consumer protection.

blocks.text: 4.2.3  The Insurance Act 2003: Strengths and Limitations

blocks.h: The Insurance Act 2003 governed the Nigerian insurance sector for over twenty years and represented a significant advance on its predecessors. Key contributions included the formalisation of the 'no premium, no cover' principle, detailed licensing requirements, mandatory separation of life and non-life funds, and corporate governance obligations. However, by the mid-2010s several structural limitations had become apparent: the minimum capital requirements (₦2 billion for life insurers, ₦3 billion for non-life) were manifestly inadequate; the regulatory framework had no provision for Insurtech; consumer protection provisions lacked enforcement teeth; and the legislation remained fragmented across multiple instruments. NIIRA 2025 addresses all of these limitations.

NAICOM was established by the National Insurance Commission Act 1997 (Decree No. 1 of 1997) as the apex regulatory authority for the Nigerian insurance industry. It is a federal government agency operating under the Federal Ministry of Finance, with operational independence in its regulatory and supervisory functions. Its powers under the 1997 Act were substantially enhanced by NIIRA 2025, which expanded its mandate to encompass Insurtech operations, consumer protection, and the Insurance Policyholders' Protection Fund.<sup>[2]</sup>

The apex regulatory authority for Nigeria's insurance sector, established by the National Insurance Commission Act 1997 and further empowered by NIIRA 2025. NAICOM oversees life, non-life, composite, reinsurance, Takaful, microinsurance, Insurtech, brokers, loss adjusters, and web aggregators. Its vision is 'A safe and stable insurance industry competing globally and contributing optimally to Nigeria's economy.'
Current Commissioner for Insurance and CEO: Mr. Olusegun Ayo Omosehin. Headquarters: Abuja.

NAICOM is governed by a Board of Commissioners comprising the Commissioner for Insurance (CEO), a Deputy Commissioner (Technical), a Deputy Commissioner (Finance and Administration), and part-time commissioners drawn from the CBN, Federal Ministry of Finance, Federal Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment, and independent representatives. Current Commissioner: Mr. Olusegun Ayo Omosehin. Deputy Commissioners: Dr. Usman Jankara Jimada and Mr. Ekerete Ola Gam-Ikon.<sup>[3]</sup>
Under NIIRA 2025 and the NAICOM Act 1997, NAICOM exercises the following principal functions:

rows: Issue, renew, suspend, and revoke licences for all categories of insurance market participant; maintain the public register of licensed operators.
Set and monitor MCRs and the RBC framework; engage independent auditors to verify capital; revoke licences for non-compliance by the July 2026 deadline.
Review and approve all new insurance products and material amendments before market launch; set premium rates for compulsory classes.
Monitor sales practices, disclosure, claims handling, and 'no premium, no cover' compliance; investigate mis-selling complaints.
Conduct routine and special examinations; require audited accounts (by 30 June annually), quarterly returns (within 10 days of quarter-end), and actuarial valuations.
Operate Consumer Complaints Bureau; adjudicate policyholder complaints; enforce 60-day claims settlement timelines; impose penalties.
Issue directives, fines, and warnings; suspend/revoke licences; take over management of distressed insurers; initiate criminal prosecution.
Promote insurance awareness and financial inclusion; foster innovation via regulatory sandbox; develop Insurtech standards.

blocks.h: Commissioner Omosehin has articulated five strategic priorities framed by the principle that 'regulation must build trust and unlock growth':<sup>[18]</sup>

items.h: Policyholder protection: Clear market conduct standards, prompt claims settlement, strong capital buffers, and credible enforcement.
Innovation enablement: Predictable, technology-friendly rules reducing barriers to digital distribution and alternative data in underwriting.
Market discipline: Competition based on sound governance, financial solvency, pricing integrity, and service quality.
Market conduct: Strengthened underwriting discipline, data-driven market surveillance, improved claims reserving, and anti-fraud measures.
Innovation and digitisation: Regulatory sandboxes; fast-track approvals for microinsurance, parametric, and embedded insurance; cybersecurity and data protection safeguards.

blocks.title: Advisory: NAICOM Engagement, Best Practices for Regulated Entities

blocks.h: Insurers that build proactive, transparent, and technically credible relationships with NAICOM consistently achieve better outcomes in licensing, product approvals, and enforcement proceedings. Best practices:

items.h: Appoint a dedicated regulatory affairs function with Board-level access. Track all NAICOM circulars, guidelines, and consultation papers; maintain a compliance calendar.
File returns ahead of deadline. Quarterly returns are due within 10 days of quarter-end; audited annual accounts by 30 June. Late filing triggers licence suspension risk.
Participate in NAICOM consultation processes. Insurers that engage through the NIA, individually, or through working groups shape their own regulatory environment.
Maintain contemporaneous records of all NAICOM correspondence. These are the insurer's primary defence in any examination, complaint, or enforcement action.
Brief the Board on regulatory developments quarterly. Under NIIRA 2025, Board members are personally accountable for regulatory compliance.

blocks.text: 4.4  NIIRA 2025: Key Provisions, Innovations, and Repealed Legislation

blocks.h: The Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act 2025 (Act No. 2, 2025) received Presidential assent on 31 July 2025. NAICOM's formal announcement was issued on 5–6 August 2025. The Act was passed by the Senate in December 2024 and the House of Representatives in March 2025, following extensive consultations with NAICOM, the NIA, NCRIB, CIIN, PenCom, and other stakeholders.<sup>[4]</sup>

Its stated objectives are: to provide a comprehensive legal and regulatory framework for insurance in Nigeria; to align Nigerian insurance regulation with international best practice; to promote financial inclusion; and to support the Federal Government's ambition of growing the Nigerian economy to USD 1 trillion by 2030.
NIIRA 2025 consolidates and repeals the following prior statutes, none of which remain in force for matters within the Act's scope:

items.h: Insurance Act, Cap. I17, LFN 2004 (Insurance Act 2003), primary insurance legislation for over twenty years.
Marine Insurance Act, Cap. M2, LFN 2004, marine insurance now absorbed into NIIRA 2025.
Motor Vehicles (Third Party Insurance) Act, Cap. M22, LFN 2004, motor third-party provisions consolidated.
National Insurance Corporation of Nigeria Act, Cap. N54, LFN 2004.
Nigeria Reinsurance Corporation Act, Cap. N131, LFN 2004.

blocks.h: Still in force (NOT repealed):

items.h: National Insurance Commission Act 1997 (NAICOM's constituting instrument).
CIIN Act No. 22 of 1993.
NCRIB Act No. 21 of 1991.
Pension Reform Act 2014 (as amended).

Risk-Based Capital (RBC) Framework: Capital must be the higher of the flat MCR or the RBC determined by NAICOM based on actual risk profile (underwriting, market, credit, operational, concentration risks). This represents a fundamental shift from the simple balance-sheet test of the Insurance Act 2003.

Raised Minimum Capital Requirements (s.15): Life ₦10bn; Non-life ₦15bn; Reinsurance ₦35bn (each the higher of the figure and risk-based capital). New composite insurer licences are no longer issued; existing composites must separate within five years (s.6). Increases of 250–400% from the 2003 Act thresholds, designed to build an industry capable of retaining larger risks domestically.

Insurtech Licensing: Dedicated licensing for Standalone Insurtechs (₦1bn life / ₦1.5bn non-life) and Partnering Insurtechs (₦10m + professional indemnity), legitimising Nigeria's growing digital insurance sector.

Enhanced Consumer Protection: Mandatory 60-day claims settlement with compound interest for delay; Insurance Policyholders' Protection Fund (Section 212); cooling-off right; proportionate remedies replacing harsh common law avoidance.
Compulsory NIN Linkage: All policies must be linked to the policyholder's National Identification Number by April 2026, enhancing fraud prevention and AML compliance.
NAICOM-BPP MoU: Legislative basis for conditioning government contract awards on insurance compliance.
Actuarial Strengthening: Annual actuarial valuations mandatory for all life insurers; statutory actuary may report directly to NAICOM if access is denied.
Mandatory Separation of Life and Non-Life Funds: Cross-subsidisation prohibited; enhanced protection for long-term policyholders.

Corporate Governance Enhancement: Board composition requirements (7–15 members; max 40% executive; at least one INED; six mandatory board committees); fit and proper standards; dividend restrictions pending NAICOM approval.
Domestic Cession Requirement: Nigerian risks must be processed by NAICOM-licensed insurers before surplus is ceded internationally, designed to retain premium domestically.

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025 establishes a comprehensive licensing architecture covering every category of insurance market participant. No person may carry on insurance business in Nigeria, or hold themselves out as doing so, without a NAICOM licence. Unlicensed insurance activity is a criminal offence.

blocks.h: The standard licensing process for a new insurance company follows a structured sequence:

items.h: Pre-application engagement with NAICOM to understand current requirements and the Commission's priorities.

Formal application: certificate of incorporation; draft memorandum and articles; business plan identifying market niche, products, and distribution; evidence of capital; details and CVs of proposed principal officers; draft risk management framework.
Fit and proper assessment of all directors and principal officers against NAICOM's criteria: financial probity, professional qualifications, relevant experience, and absence of disqualifying history.
Provisional licence (approval in principle) issued subject to completing all pre-commencement requirements: physical establishment, system readiness, capital injection, statutory deposit with CBN.
Full operating licence issued upon satisfaction of all pre-commencement requirements. Annual renewal conditional on continued compliance.

blocks.text: 4.6  Capital Requirements and the Risk-Based Capital Framework

blocks.h: Section 15 of NIIRA 2025 establishes the minimum capital requirements (MCR) for all licensed insurance operators:
Sources: NIIRA 2025, Section 15; NAICOM Circular 13 August 2025; BusinessDay (August 2025); The Revealer (January 2026).<sup>[11]</sup><sup>[12]</sup>

Section 15(1) of NIIRA 2025 provides that an insurer must maintain the higher of the flat MCR or the risk-based capital (RBC) determined by NAICOM. The RBC framework takes into account: underwriting risk; market risk; credit risk; operational risk; and concentration risk. This aligns Nigeria with the Solvency II standard and the IAIS Insurance Core Principles (ICP 17: Capital Adequacy). Under RBC, a larger or more complex insurer with a concentrated or volatile portfolio may be required to hold significantly more capital than the flat MCR, while a conservatively managed insurer whose risk profile is modest may need only the flat minimum. NAICOM retains discretion under Section 15(8) to increase requirements beyond the MCR for individual insurers based on size, complexity, or risk profile.

blocks.title: Advisory: The Recapitalisation Opportunity, Strategic Options for Life Insurers

blocks.h: Life insurers facing the ₦10 billion MCR have five principal strategic paths to compliance:

items.h: Rights issue or public offer: Existing shareholders contribute additional capital proportionately. Preserves ownership structure. Requires active shareholders with capital appetite and SEC fast-track process.
Private placement: New strategic investors subscribe to shares at an agreed valuation. May bring not just capital but technical expertise, distribution networks, or technology platform access.
Merger with or acquisition of another insurer: Combines capital bases; creates economies of scale and potentially market leadership. Requires NAICOM approval; integration risk significant.

Foreign strategic investment: International insurers (South African groups [Sanlam, Old Mutual], pan-African players [Allianz Africa, AXA], or Gulf-based capital) have historically provided recapitalisation capital. NIIRA 2025 permits foreign ownership subject to fit and proper requirements.

Operational restructuring before capital-raising: Identify and realise latent asset values (investment property revaluation, debt recovery, portfolio rationalisation) to maximise admissible capital before external capital is sought.

blocks.h: Compulsory insurance is insurance that Nigerian law requires individuals, employers, or businesses to obtain as a condition of operating, owning property, or conducting specified activities. The rationale is social: certain risks (particularly those where the potential victim of an adverse event has no power to protect herself) are too important to be left to voluntary market decisions. NIIRA 2025 preserves and strengthens the compulsory insurance framework and creates more effective enforcement mechanisms through NAICOM's expanded powers and the NAICOM-BPP MoU.

rows: NIIRA 2025 (consolidating Motor Vehicles (Third Party Insurance) Act). Every vehicle on a public road must be insured for third-party bodily injury and death. Enforced by FRSC, Police, and NAICOM online verification.
Employees' Compensation Act 2010; NIIRA 2025. Employers with three or more employees must insure liability for workplace injury, disease, or death. Administered by NSITF.
NIIRA 2025. Owners of public buildings (offices, schools, markets, hotels, recreational facilities) must insure third-party injury or death on their premises. Minimum ₦1m per person.
NIIRA 2025; Medical and Dental Practitioners Act. All licensed healthcare professionals (doctors, dentists, nurses, pharmacists) must maintain professional indemnity insurance before practising.
NIIRA 2025 (consolidating Marine Insurance Act). All goods imported into or exported from Nigeria must be insured with a NAICOM-licensed insurer, retaining marine premium domestically.
Pension Reform Act 2014 (as amended). Employers with five or more PRA-enrolled employees must maintain group life cover providing a minimum three times annual salary on death in service.
NIIRA 2025. Owners and contractors of buildings under construction of two or more floors must insure third-party liability from construction activity.
Civil Aviation Act. All commercial airlines and charter operators must maintain passenger liability insurance at prescribed minimum levels.

blocks.h: Historically, enforcement of compulsory insurance in Nigeria has been weak. Fake third-party certificates, falsified group life cover notes, and expired building insurance are endemic. NIIRA 2025 addresses enforcement through multiple channels:

items.h: NAICOM direct enforcement: Market raids, business premises checks, and coordination with sector regulators.

NAICOM-BPP MoU: Integrates NAICOM's verification system with the Bureau of Public Procurement's contractor pre-qualification. No Federal Government contract without current, valid insurance compliance.
FRSC and Police: Verify motor third-party insurance at checkpoints using NAICOM's online portal. Fake or expired certificates are electronically detectable.
Ministry of Labour: Enforces employers' liability insurance compliance.
State and local government inspectors: Enforce occupiers' liability and public building insurance at premises level.

blocks.h: NAICOM and the Organised Private Sector of Nigeria (OPSN) are actively developing sector-specific enforcement frameworks for the maritime and petroleum sectors, following a March 2026 engagement at which the Commissioner confirmed NAICOM's responsibility for issuing frameworks and premium determinations for compulsory insurance products in these sectors.<sup>[17]</sup>

blocks.text: 4.8  The Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria (CIIN)

blocks.h: The CIIN traces its origins to 1959, when a small group of practitioners, a mix of expatriates and their Nigerian counterparts, established the Insurance Institute of Nigeria (IIN). The IIN was affiliated to the Chartered Insurance Institute (CII) of London in 1960, adopting the CII's examination structure and professional standards. On 26 February 1993, the Institute was elevated to chartered status by Decree (now Act) No. 22 of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, the CIIN Act 1993, which gave it the statutory mandate to determine the standards of knowledge and skill required of persons seeking to become registered members of the insurance profession in Nigeria.<sup>[13]</sup>

The statutory professional body for insurance practitioners in Nigeria, established under CIIN Act No. 22 of 1993 (formerly the Insurance Institute of Nigeria, founded 1959). The CIIN sets professional qualification standards, administers examinations, registers practitioners, and promotes CPD across the Nigerian insurance industry. Its College of Insurance and Financial Management (CIFM) provides post-graduate and executive education.
Current President: Mrs. Yetunde Ilori. Headquarters: Lagos. Affiliation: Chartered Insurance Institute (CII), London.

rows: Certificate of Proficiency (COP): statutory requirement under NIIRA 2025; Certificate in Insurance (Cert. CIIN)
COP: Short qualification mandatory for all licensed insurance agents. Cert. CIIN: 5 core subjects. Insurance Principles, Insurance Law, Life Assurance, General Insurance, and Healthcare Insurance.
Diploma in Insurance (Dip. CIIN); Designation on passing: AIIN (Associate Insurance Institute of Nigeria)
8–10 subjects including advanced underwriting, claims, reinsurance, broking, and risk management. Minimum professional standard for insurance managers and senior brokers.
ACII (through CII London pathway, recognised by CIIN); FIIN (Fellow of the Insurance Institute of Nigeria, highest CIIN designation)
FIIN awarded to members demonstrating sustained senior-level contribution. ACII is the equivalent London CII qualification; both are internationally portable.

blocks.text: 4.8.3  NIIRA 2025 Requirements Relating to CIIN Qualification

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025 substantially elevates the mandatory role of CIIN qualification:<sup>[14]</sup>

items.h: Individual insurance agents: Must be licensed by NAICOM and, under s.37(2) of NIIRA 2025, hold a CIIN Certificate of Proficiency, have at least 10 years’ experience or length of service in an underwriting firm, have no conviction for dishonesty or fraud, and not have been bankrupt in the preceding five years. The licence is renewable after three years (s.37(8)). Operating without NAICOM licence: fine up to ₦500,000 and/or six months' imprisonment.
Corporate insurance agents: At least one principal officer must hold the CIIN COP (s.37(2)(b)).
Insurance brokers: Principal officers of licensed brokerages must meet NCRIB qualification standards, which require CIIN Diploma-level qualification for senior positions.

Insurers (key officers): Fit and proper requirements under NIIRA 2025 encompass professional qualifications, including CIIN membership at the appropriate level for underwriting and actuarial officers.

blocks.h: CIIN qualification has moved from a desirable professional credential to a statutory prerequisite for market access. Practitioners who have not yet obtained their CIIN qualification should do so urgently. The CIIN College of Insurance and Financial Management (CIFM) offers flexible study programmes including weekend classes, distance learning, and intensive revision courses.

Alongside NAICOM as the statutory regulator and CIIN as the professional body, four industry associations represent specific participant categories, advance collective interests, and perform self-regulatory functions that complement statutory oversight.

The Nigerian Insurers Association is the umbrella trade body for all licensed insurance and reinsurance companies in Nigeria, founded in 1971. The NIA represents its members in engagements with NAICOM, the Federal Government, and international bodies including the African Insurance Organisation (AIO). It compiles and publishes the Annual Statistical Bulletin, the primary source of industry-wide market data, and administers the Nigerian Insurance Industry Claims Verification System (NIICVS) to combat cross-insurer fraud.<sup>[15]</sup>

The NIA's current chairman, Kunle Ahmed, has described NIIRA 2025 as 'a pivotal legislation that sets the stage for transformative progress across the insurance ecosystem.' All licensed insurers and reinsurers are members; membership is effectively a market requirement given the NIA's role in regulatory consultations and industry advocacy.

blocks.text: 4.9.2  Nigerian Council of Registered Insurance Brokers (NCRIB)

blocks.h: The NCRIB is the statutory body responsible for regulating the professional conduct of insurance brokers. Established by NCRIB Act No. 21 of 1991, the Council has exclusive powers to regulate both individual and corporate insurance broker members. All NAICOM-licensed insurance brokers must be NCRIB members; NCRIB acts as a first-line regulator for the broking profession, administering its own code of conduct, CPD requirements, and disciplinary proceedings. The current NCRIB President, Prince Babatunde Oguntade, has welcomed NIIRA 2025 as a framework that 'ensures seamless and ethical business operations between brokers and underwriters while sanctioning charlatans operating in the insurance industry.'<sup>[16]</sup>

blocks.text: 4.9.3  Institute of Loss Adjusters of Nigeria (ILAN)

blocks.h: ILAN represents loss adjusters: the independent claim investigators and valuers who assess and quantify insured losses. Loss adjusters provide neutral valuations that protect both the insurer (against inflated claims) and the insured (against under-settlement). ILAN maintains professional standards, administers the AILA (Associate of the Institute of Loss Adjusters) qualification, and provides CPD for members. All licensed loss adjusters must be ILAN members and NAICOM-registered.

blocks.text: 4.9.4  Association of Registered Insurance Agents of Nigeria (ARIAN)

blocks.h: ARIAN is the trade body for individual insurance agents, the largest single distribution category in Nigeria. ARIAN promotes the professional interests of its members, advocates in regulatory consultations, and works with CIIN and NAICOM on training and CPD frameworks. Membership is compulsory for all NAICOM-registered individual agents. Given NIIRA 2025's raised COP licensing standard for agents, ARIAN has a significant educational and transition management role.

rows: Pan-continental industry body representing African insurers. Annual conference is the continent's premier insurance gathering.
Nigerian life insurers participate; AIO data provides continental market benchmarks.
College of Insurance and Financial Management (CIFM)
Subsidiary of CIIN; post-graduate, executive, and professional insurance education.
Primary provider of CIIN examination preparation courses and CPD programmes for all Nigerian practitioners.
State-linked domestic reinsurer restructured under NIIRA 2025; provides facultative and treaty reinsurance capacity.
Key domestic reinsurer for life insurers' group life and credit life treaty programmes.
Pan-African private reinsurer headquartered in Lagos.
Major treaty reinsurance partner for Nigerian life insurers, particularly in group life.
Regulates the Contributory Pension Scheme. Not an insurance body but intersects with life insurers at the Group Life mandate and Retirement Life Annuity junction.
Every life insurer underwriting Group Life (PRA-compliant) and RLA must be PenCom-approved and compliant.

blocks.text: 4.10  NAICOM Prudential Guidelines and Key Regulatory Instruments

blocks.h: In addition to NIIRA 2025, the regulatory landscape is shaped by secondary instruments, guidelines, circulars, directives, and bulletins issued by NAICOM under its statutory powers. These do not require legislative process; they take immediate regulatory effect. Practitioners must maintain current awareness of NAICOM's secondary regulatory output, published on naicom.gov.ng. Key standing guidelines include:

items.h: NAICOM Prudential Guidelines for Insurers and Reinsurers in Nigeria (effective July 2015, as amended): Capital management, investment, reinsurance, and risk management standards, now updated by NIIRA 2025.

Corporate Governance Guidelines for Insurance and Reinsurance Companies (CGGIRC) 2021: Board composition, committee structure, fit and proper standards, and disclosure. Enhanced by NIIRA 2025's statutory corporate governance provisions.
NAICOM Guidelines for Insurtech Operations in Nigeria (effective 1 August 2025): Full treatment in Chapter 28.
NAICOM Guidelines for Micro-Insurance Operations: Simplified licensing, product, and distribution standards.
NAICOM Guidelines on Regulation of Insurance Brokers: Minimum capital, client money segregation, remittance timelines.
NAICOM Takaful Guidelines: Governance of non-interest (Takaful) insurance operations, full treatment in Chapter 9.
NAICOM Recapitalisation Guidelines (August 2025): Implementation framework for MCR compliance, admissible assets, verification process.

blocks.h: The MoU between NAICOM and the Bureau of Public Procurement (BPP), finalised in 2026, integrates NAICOM's online insurance verification system with the BPP's contractor pre-qualification process. No Federal Government contractor or supplier may receive a contract award, payment, or licence renewal without demonstrating current and valid insurance compliance. This represents one of the most effective enforcement mechanisms yet established: it conditions access to government revenue on insurance compliance. The MoU is expected to serve as a model for similar agreements with state governments and sector regulators.<sup>[20]</sup>

blocks.text: 4.10.3  The NHIA Act 2022 and Its Intersection with Life Insurance

blocks.h: The National Health Insurance Authority Act 2022 abolished the NHIS and made health insurance mandatory for all Nigerians, the single largest extension of compulsory insurance in Nigerian regulatory history. For life insurers, this creates both intersection and opportunity:<sup>[19]</sup>

items.h: Health riders on life policies: Life insurers offering hospitalisation cash, critical illness, and medical reimbursement riders must ensure their products do not conflict with NHIA's basic health benefit package in ways that confuse policyholders.
HMO overlap: NHIA-regulated HMOs underwrite products economically similar to life health riders. NAICOM and NHIA are working to clarify the regulatory boundary between their respective domains.
Group scheme design: Group life policies that include health benefit components must be structured to avoid duplicating compulsory NHIA contributions in a manner that creates employer confusion.

Critical illness opportunity: With NHIA providing a basic health benefit floor, the gap in the market for lump-sum critical illness cover, paying on diagnosis of serious conditions beyond NHIA's coverage, may widen significantly. Life insurers are well-positioned to serve this need.

blocks.h: This chapter has surveyed the full architecture of insurance regulation in Nigeria from colonial origins through the landmark reforms of NIIRA 2025. The following are the essential propositions.

items.h: Insurance regulation in Nigeria has evolved through six major legislative milestones from independence to the present day, culminating in NIIRA 2025, which received presidential assent on 31 July 2025 and is the most comprehensive insurance legislation in the country's history.

NAICOM is the apex regulatory authority. Its mandate encompasses licensing, capital supervision, product approval, market conduct, consumer protection, enforcement, and development. Commissioner Omosehin has articulated five strategic priorities guiding the Commission through 2030: policyholder protection; innovation enablement; market discipline; market conduct; and digitisation.

NIIRA 2025 consolidates and repeals five prior insurance statutes. Key innovations include RBC alongside flat MCRs, raised minimum capital requirements (₦10bn life, ₦15bn non-life, ₦35bn reinsurance), 60-day claims settlement (Insurtech licensing and NIN linkage come from NAICOM regulation and guidelines, not the Act), and the Insurance Policyholders' Protection Fund.

The licensing regime under NIIRA 2025 covers fourteen categories of market participant. The process requires incorporation, capital adequacy, fit and proper assessment, and NAICOM approval of key officers.

The recapitalisation programme commenced 31 July 2025 with a deadline of 30 July 2026. As of January 2026, 17–21 of 58 operators had met the new requirements. PwC, KPMG, Deloitte, and EY are conducting independent verification. No extension to the deadline.
Seven compulsory insurance classes exist under Nigerian law. Enforcement is being strengthened through NAICOM's expanded powers, the NAICOM-BPP MoU, and digital verification systems.

The CIIN, established 1959 and chartered 1993, sets professional qualification standards for all practitioners. NIIRA 2025 (s.37(2)) makes the CIIN COP, together with at least 10 years’ experience or service in an underwriting firm, a statutory prerequisite for an individual insurance agent; for a corporate agent, at least one principal officer must hold the COP.
The industry association ecosystem (NIA [trade body for insurers], NCRIB [brokers], ILAN [loss adjusters], ARIAN [agents]) performs complementary self-regulatory and advocacy roles alongside NAICOM.

NAICOM's Prudential Guidelines, Corporate Governance Guidelines, Insurtech Guidelines, Takaful Guidelines, and Recapitalisation Guidelines form an essential secondary regulatory framework alongside NIIRA 2025.

The NHIA Act 2022's mandatory health insurance obligation creates intersection with life insurer health riders and critical illness products, and generates both compliance obligations and new market opportunities.

blocks.h: National Insurance Commission. The apex statutory regulatory authority for Nigeria's insurance sector, established by the National Insurance Commission Act 1997 and empowered by NIIRA 2025. Current Commissioner: Mr. Olusegun Ayo Omosehin.

Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act 2025 (Act No. 2, 2025). Presidential assent 31 July 2025. Consolidates and repeals five prior insurance statutes. The primary legislative framework for insurance in Nigeria.
The flat minimum capital an insurer must maintain under NIIRA 2025. Life: ₦10bn; Non-life: ₦15bn; Reinsurance: ₦35bn (s.15). Insurers must maintain the higher of MCR and RBC.

A capital adequacy framework requiring insurers to hold capital proportionate to their actual risk profile (underwriting, market, credit, operational, concentration risks). Introduced by NIIRA 2025 as a dual standard alongside the flat MCR.
NAICOM-supervised exercise requiring 58 operators to achieve NIIRA 2025 MCR compliance by 30 July 2026. Plans submitted 30 September 2025; independent verification by PwC, KPMG, Deloitte, EY.
Section 212 of NIIRA 2025. Funded by a 0.25% levy on the gross premium income of every insurer and reinsurer. Compensates policyholders of insolvent insurers, the insurance sector's NDIC equivalent.

Insurance required by law as a condition of operating, owning, or conducting specified activities. Seven compulsory classes under Nigerian law: motor third-party, employers' liability, occupiers' liability, healthcare professional indemnity, marine (import/export), group life, and public building liability.

Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria Act No. 22 of 1993. Statutory basis for the CIIN's mandate to set professional qualification standards. NIIRA 2025 references CIIN COP as a statutory prerequisite for agent licensing.
Foundation-level professional qualification of the CIIN; now a statutory prerequisite for licensing as an insurance agent under NIIRA 2025.

Memorandum of Understanding between NAICOM and the Bureau of Public Procurement conditioning all Federal Government contract awards on current, valid insurance compliance, a major new compulsory insurance enforcement mechanism.

National Health Insurance Authority Act 2022. Makes health insurance mandatory for all Nigerians; creates intersection with NAICOM-regulated health riders on life policies and opportunities in the critical illness market.
Nigerian Insurers Association. Umbrella trade body for all licensed insurers and reinsurers since 1971. Publishes the industry annual statistical report and administers the NIICVS fraud database.
Nigerian Council of Registered Insurance Brokers. Statutory self-regulatory body for insurance brokers. NCRIB Act No. 21 of 1991. Membership compulsory for all NAICOM-licensed brokers.
Institute of Loss Adjusters of Nigeria. Professional body for loss adjusters. Membership compulsory for all NAICOM-registered loss adjusters.
Association of Registered Insurance Agents of Nigeria. Trade body for individual insurance agents. Membership compulsory for all NAICOM-registered individual agents.
